hero.title: Coursera Specialization Structure
hero.subtitle: A Specialization is a set of related courses, each built to stand on its own and be reused.
hero.hint: Click any element below to learn more about it.

specialization.label: SPECIALIZATION
specialization.rail: A set of related courses that together help learners master one competency.
specialization.definition: A series of related, in-depth courses that help learners master a competency.
specialization.outcome: Learners who complete every course in the Specialization earn a Specialization Certificate.

detail.title: Specialization
body: A Specialization is a series of related, in-depth courses that help learners master a competency. Specializations include projects — authentic, hands-on assessments with real-world applications that let learners demonstrate the skill.
Learners who complete every course earn a Specialization Certificate. Learners who complete a single course earn a course certificate for that course alone.
Design it as a coherent set rather than a fixed path. Learners can enroll in any course in any order, and a well-built course may later be reused in a different Specialization.
tips: Name the competency the whole set adds up to before planning individual courses.
Plan for 3–4 courses and 12–32 hours of total learner time.
Every course must work for someone who takes only that one course.
Each course should include at least one hands-on project. Plan where those live early — they're expected, not optional.
Put high-level learning objectives on the Specialization landing page, then chunk them into course- and module-level objectives.

courses.label: COURSES
courses.rail: Each course is anchored to specific, demonstrable skills. Courses are not chapters — any one of them may be reused in another Specialization later.

callout.title: Standalone does not mean unsequenced
callout.body: You can absolutely design courses and modules that increase in complexity — that's good pedagogy. What breaks reuse is cross-referencing. Don't reference other courses, modules, or the Specialization by name or number. Establish the context fresh inside each piece instead, and it works whether a learner arrives first or last.

detail.title: Course
body: Courses give learners access to instructional videos, assessments, and other learning content. Learners who pay for and complete a course earn a shareable course certificate.

Anchor each course to clearly defined skills — concrete, demonstrable abilities tied to real work, like "clean and validate a dataset" or "build a responsive web page layout." Content that is clearly skill-aligned is easier for learners to find and easier for your team to reuse.
Build every course as a self-contained unit. Anyone can enroll in any course at any time, and your team may want to place this course in a different Specialization later.
tips: Anchor to skills, not topics — name the ability a learner walks away with.
Target 2–4 learning objectives, 3–4 modules, and 2–8 hours of learning.
State needed background as a skill, not as another course a learner should have taken.

Keep supporting files (glossaries, templates, setup guides) inside readings and activities in the learning path — not in the course Resources section, which doesn't travel with content when it's reused.
Put the syllabus and orienting context on the course landing page so modules can focus purely on teaching.

modules.label: MODULES
modules.rail: A module is a self-contained section of a course, built around a single skill or topic.
modules.note: Title each module for the skill it teaches — "Identifying and Handling Missing Data," not "Module 1: Introduction." Coursera adds the numbering, and your own numbers break when a module moves.

cards.title: Module
cards.role: One skill or topic, taught end to end.

detail.title: Module
body: A module is one self-contained section of a course. Modules make up the course structure, and learners work through them at their own pace on personalized deadlines.
Each module is built around a single skill, carries its own 2–4 learning objectives, and ends with at least one graded assessment that checks those objectives.

Every module also needs a module description. Learners see it as a message from you, so write it conversationally and address them directly — introduce what the module covers, highlight the objectives, and offer a tip for success.
tips: Title the module for its skill. The platform supplies the number.
Open each module by establishing its own context — a learner should never need to have seen anything else first.
Structure the module with the WWHAA pattern below.
If a learner needs background, say what they should already know, not where they should have learned it.
Your first module is the strongest chance to hook learners. Make it a full teaching module rather than a syllabus walkthrough.

lessons.label: LESSONS
lessons.rail: Lessons are an optional way to group related content inside a module.
lessons.definition: Lessons group related items within a module. They're optional — use them when a module has enough content that grouping helps learners find their way.

detail.title: Lesson
body: A lesson is an optional grouping layer inside a module. Lessons let you cluster related items so a longer module is easier for learners to navigate.
You don't have to use them. A module with only a handful of items usually reads better without them.
tips: Group by idea, not by format — don't build a "videos" lesson and a "readings" lesson.
Start a new lesson when the sub-topic changes or a learner would naturally pause.
If a module only has a few items, skip lessons entirely.

assets.label: LEARNING ASSETS
assets.rail: Modules and lessons contain a mix of assets that teach, let learners practice, and check what they've learned.
assets.alsoAvailable: Also available: in-video questions, code blocks, programming assignments, Coursera Labs, AI-graded assignments, and external tools via LTI.

detail.title: Video
body: Videos introduce and teach a course topic. Video is powerful for human connection, storytelling, and demonstration — the moments where learners benefit from seeing a real person.

Chunking is the whole game. Three to six minutes is optimal for retention, and videos under 10 minutes increase lecture completion rates by 16% while raising satisfaction with the course overall. Longer videos often get skipped entirely.
The strongest-performing courses keep at least two-thirds of their videos under 10 minutes. Break complex topics into a series of short, focused videos with clear, specific titles.
tips: Aim under 7 minutes; 6 or less is ideal. One idea per video.
What raises engagement: open with a hook or story, keep the tone conversational, use appropriate humour, add visuals or animation, and keep a relatively brisk speaking pace.
Don't default to video. Readings, interactives, and labs are often better for reference material and anything that needs frequent updating.
Use AI tools to speed up production, but don't make AI the on-screen presenter — learners benefit from seeing real people.
Accessibility: every video needs accurate captions and a transcript.
In-video questions can pause a video to prompt a quick check.

cards.title: Reading
cards.short: Articles or guides that deepen understanding.

detail.title: Reading
body: Learner-facing text used to explain, extend, or provide reference material. Best for anything learners will want to scan, search, or return to later.
Readings are also the right home for supporting files — glossaries, templates, setup guides — because items in the learning path travel with your content when it's reused.
tips: Provide the complete text, not an outline.
Accessibility: describe every image in alt text, use real headings for structure, and write descriptive link text rather than "click here."
Copyright: confirm you have permission for every image, figure, and excerpt, and attribute sources.
Good for reference material, worked examples, and step-by-step instructions.

detail.title: Audio podcast
body: A recognised instructional format on Coursera alongside video and readings. Audio suits interviews, expert conversations, and narrative explanation — anything a learner might absorb while commuting or walking.
It's also considerably faster and cheaper to produce than video, which makes it a practical way to add variety to a module.
tips: Best for conversation, storytelling, and expert perspective — not for anything visual.
Accessibility: a full transcript is required, since there's no visual channel at all.
Keep episodes focused on one idea, same as video.
Don't use audio for content learners will need to reference later — use a reading.

cards.title: Interactive Plugin
cards.short: Embedded web apps for interactive practice.

detail.title: Interactive plugin
body: Plugins embed single-page web applications directly inside a Coursera course item, so they support nearly any experience the web can deliver — simulations, visualisers, calculators, explorable diagrams.
They're built by third parties including university partners, independent developers, and researchers. They can be ungraded, used as graded assignment questions, or wired to external tools.
tips: Strong choice for concepts that are easier to manipulate than to describe.
Confirm feasibility early — plugins usually need development effort your team has to plan for.
Accessibility: interactive content needs keyboard operability and screen-reader labels. Check before committing.
Related options: code blocks, JavaScript plugins, and external tools via LTI.

cards.title: Coach Dialogue
cards.short: AI-driven conversation that applies and reflects.

detail.title: Coach Dialogue
body: Dialogue items let you create AI-driven discussions that simulate interaction with a live instructor, leading learners through structured, text-based conversations designed to hit specific learning objectives.

The AI guide (Coursera Coach) helps learners think critically and apply concepts to real-world situations by asking adaptive, open-ended questions, tailored to each learner with personalised feedback.
Coursera recommends at least one Dialogue item per course, and notes that including one improves learner engagement.
tips: Write the coach goal: what should the learner think through, decide, or produce?
Provide an opening question, 2–4 follow-up areas, and a closing reflection.
Best for reflection, case analysis, ethical decisions, and complex problem-solving.
Ungraded unless you specify otherwise.
A Dialogue in the first module is a strong way to connect the topic to a learner's own goals.

detail.title: Hands-on practice
body: Where learners try the skill directly with no stakes. This can be an off-platform activity with step-by-step instructions, an ungraded Coursera Lab, or in-browser coding.
Ungraded Labs allow trial-and-error learning with immediate feedback and no formal assessment — sandbox environments for exploration without grade pressure.
tips: Provide the activity plus step-by-step learner instructions and any setup details.
Labs need notebooks or files plus environment details — confirm feasibility early.
Structure activities around clear deliverables so completion can be assessed.
No stakes. This is where learners get to fail safely.

detail.title: Practice quiz — assessment for learning
body: Practice assessments are assessment for learning: optional, ungraded, and not counted toward a learner's final grade. They help learners self-assess, catch misconceptions early, and build the confidence to apply a skill for real.
They're also your best chance to give meaningful feedback while a learner is still forming their understanding.
Coursera recommends at least one practice quiz and one practice activity per module.
tips: Provide every question, the correct answers, and feedback for both correct and incorrect responses.
Feedback should help learners identify the error, not just mark it wrong.
Rehearse the same thinking the graded assessment will ask for.
Use them generously — they cost a learner nothing.

detail.title: Graded assessment — assessment of learning
body: Graded assessments are assessment of learning: required, counted toward the final grade, and used to evaluate whether learners actually achieved the stated objectives.

Every module needs at least one, and every course-level objective should be validated somewhere in the graded assessments. Regular graded checkpoints give learners timely confirmation of progress instead of one high-stakes bottleneck at the end.
Coursera also recommends at least one graded project per course — an authentic, hands-on assessment with real-world application that learners can put in a portfolio.
tips: Must map to the module's stated learning objectives — not trivia from a reading.
A 10-question auto-graded quiz with answer-specific feedback is the common default.
Point learners to the specific review material for anything they missed.
For projects, AI-graded assignments and programming assignments can evaluate a submitted artifact.

wwhaa.title: Structure every module with WWHAA
wwhaa.intro: Coursera recommends the Why → What → How → Apply → Assess pattern for each module. It creates a complete, self-contained learning cycle — which is exactly what makes a module reusable somewhere else.

phases.headline: Establish real-world relevance
phases.body: Show the learner why this skill matters before teaching it. In a first module, this replaces the traditional course introduction entirely.
phases.formats: Instructor video, real-world scenario, Coach Dialogue

phases.headline: Teach key concepts
phases.body: Introduce the essential ideas the skill rests on — the minimum a learner needs before they can try it.
phases.formats: Reading, short video, graphic, audio podcast

phases.headline: Bridge theory and practice
phases.body: Show the skill actually being performed. Demonstration is what turns a concept into something a learner can picture doing.

phases.headline: Practice in realistic scenarios
phases.body: Let learners try it with no stakes and get feedback while it's still cheap to be wrong.
phases.formats: Hands-on activity, lab, Dialogue, practice quiz

phases.headline: Validate learning
phases.body: Check whether the module's objectives were met, and point learners to review material for anything missed.

notes.title: Choose the format that fits the phase
notes.body: WWHAA guides format decisions too. Don't default to video for everything — pick what serves the goal of that phase.

notes.title: Never more than two of the same type in a row
notes.body: Varied sequences — video, then reading, then practice activity — sustain engagement. Coursera's internal research shows learners drop off at significantly higher rates in repetitive sequences.

phrasing.title: Write it so it can be reused
phrasing.intro: Reuse breaks on phrasing more often than on structure. Every item should open by establishing its own context — a learner should never need to have seen anything else first.

rows.dont: "Now that you've mastered the basics from Module 1, let's apply those concepts to…"
rows.do: "Data transformation is essential for analysis. Let's explore how to use SQL functions to…"

rows.dont: "As part of this Data Science Specialization, you'll use these skills in the capstone project…"
rows.do: "These data preprocessing skills are essential for any machine learning project. Let's practice with a real dataset…"

rows.dont: "In the previous lesson, we explored how to optimize this code…"

rows.do: "This concept is fundamental to understanding how databases work…"
"This module assumes familiarity with basic SQL queries."

responsibilities.title: Copyright and accessibility
responsibilities.intro: These apply to every asset you build, and they're far cheaper to handle while drafting than after production. Duke-specific guidance will be added here.

groups.label: Copyright
items: Confirm you have permission for every image, figure, video clip, dataset, and excerpt that isn't yours.
Attribute sources, and keep a record of what you cleared and where it came from.
Course content reaches a global public audience — classroom fair-use reasoning generally doesn't carry over.
Content may be reused in another Specialization later, so permissions need to cover more than one course.

groups.label: Accessibility
items: Video needs accurate captions and a transcript. Audio needs a transcript.
Describe every meaningful image in alt text; mark purely decorative images as decorative.
Don't rely on colour alone to carry meaning, and check contrast on slides and graphics.
Use real headings and lists so screen readers can navigate a reading's structure.
Write descriptive link text rather than "click here."
Interactive plugins and labs need keyboard operability — verify before committing to one.

comparison.title: How this differs from a for-credit course
comparison.intro: Most of the surprises in a first Coursera build come from assumptions carried over from semester teaching.

rows.coursera: No schedule. Learners start any day and work at their own pace on personalized deadlines.

rows.credit: You're in the room; you can adjust live
rows.coursera: Fully asynchronous. Everything a learner needs has to already be in the course.
Anyone can enroll in any course, in any order. Prerequisites are stated, not enforced.

rows.credit: Courses build on each other within a program
rows.coursera: Courses are modular. A course may be reused in a different Specialization.
2–8 hours of learning per course; 12–32 hours across the whole Specialization.
Working adults worldwide, widely varied backgrounds, mostly self-motivated.
Mostly auto-graded. At least one graded assessment per module.

rows.credit: Grades and tuition keep students enrolled
rows.coursera: Nothing holds anyone. Every module has to earn the next click.

completion.title: Certificates
completion.body: Learners who complete a single course earn a shareable course certificate for that course. Learners who complete every course in the Specialization earn a Specialization Certificate that recognises the full competency.

handoff.title: Ready to plan yours?
handoff.body: The template is the blank version of everything above — no guidance, just the fields your design team needs. Come back here any time you want a refresher.
